Komani in the Dark

By: Sasha Schwendenwein | Commission

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
30 days without electricity is a nightmare for matric exam students, but it's also a matter of life and death for those dependent on life-saving equipment in hospitals and refrigerated medications at

Unique Selling Point:
We have an insider at the hospital willing to confirm the death of the children.

As per my treatment we will be focussing on a specific area of Queenstown- toptown and we will tell the story from there where the hospital and old age home is. Blue rise is nextdoor where our student lives, so its geographically where our story will be told from.

The frontier hospital will have an undercover where I'll walk in and film the areas the doctor points me to. And we'll also visit the old age home nextdoor.

Komani's infrastructure is rapidly deteriorating, with some areas now enduring power outages for as long as 24 days. This ongoing crisis is the result of years of neglect and mismanagement, compounded by the misallocation of equitable share grants, which have been primarily used to pay Eskom. Since 2020, the municipality's Eskom debt has skyrocketed from R350 million to an eye-watering R1.4 billion. As a result, a large portion of the municipality's funds is now consumed by debt repayment and staff salaries, leaving little for critical service delivery.

I spoke with several key local figures to better understand the situation, including community leader Alasdair McDonald, journalist Bongie Solundwa, and Jacques van Zyl, head of the local business forum. They all pointed to a deeply troubling reality.

The heart of the problem lies in the failure of three key electrical cables that supply power to Top Town, where the Water Works are located. Without power, the pumps cannot deliver water to the town, exacerbating the crisis. One of these cables also supplies power to Frontier Hospital, which has been without electricity and is now relying on backup generators to stay operational. The nearby Madeira Old Age Home is also struggling without power. Just a few days ago, there was a dramatic explosion, and we have footage of this incident, which has been shared with Chwayitisa.

The situation has worsened over the last 3.5 weeks, with a series of electrical explosions caused by overloaded cables. In an attempt to address the issue, the municipality has been adding new sections of cable to the existing infrastructure. However, this patchwork approach has only led to more frequent failures. A key issue is the lack of protection systems in the substations—when a fault occurs, it doesn’t just affect one area; it trips the entire town's power grid. This not only disrupts daily life but also inflicts serious and lasting damage to an already fragile infrastructure, further jeopardizing the town's ability to function.

What is the current plan? The municipality's current plan involves bringing in new cable sections to extend the old infrastructure, but this is essentially just delaying inevitable failures further down the line. The frequency of electrical explosions has been overwhelming—it's a clear indication of the grid’s collapse.



Summary:
MAIN CHARACTERS RESEARCH:
Daniel Lombard “Doc” – hidden identity interview. He is specializing at Frontier hospital, located in Top Town. Doc is in the surgical department. The children died in the paediatric ward.
1. Two babies were on ventilators when the generators failed, and both died – he has spoken to the 2 doctors and 2 nurses who were there. Obviously, everyone is scared and none of them will speak.Doc says the hospital head has told everyone to be quiet. But essentially they had no oxygen, because the ventilators were switched off
2. He says the lack of electricity has been difficult in a situation where they already have nothing
a. They have no working toilets in the entire hospital
b. No catheters
c. No sutra material
d. No linen – meaning the operating theatres can only do one surgery a day
3. I suggested I do a walk through of the hospital and film all of this – he will make me a map and take photos today of all the issues for me
4. He wants to speak because he says he has patients he has to send home because he simply can’t do his job. The pharmacy isn’t able to operate without electricity – so over the weekends there’s literally no medication available for patients – patients have to wait until Monday. He’s beyond frustrated and makes him want to leave, cos he’s afraid of more patients dying
Nangamso Ncobo, Matric student at Queens College, lives in Blue Rise.
1. November began the "hard" exams, but electricity outages started – she’s looking to get into University because her marks are good enough, but at home she’s had to study via candles, and she has to buy almost everyday cos they burn out fast. She also can’t charge her phone for past exam papers, so it’s become extremely challenging.
2. Only place to charge phone was at school, adding extra pressure.
3. Some mornings, no time to iron clothes due to electricity outages.
4. After writing 3-hour exams, would return home, nap, and wake up to darkness, reducing motivation to study.
5. Studying with candles, torches, or paraffin lights feels insufficient.
6. Difficult to adjust to daily life without electricity during final exams.
7. She also can’t wash herself properly because there’s no hot water, and some people don’t have water because the water pumps require electricity.
Alasdair Mcdonald, community leader.
1. He’ll talk about the current electricity issues - Komani's infrastructure is rapidly deteriorating, with some areas now enduring power outages for as long as 30 days now. This ongoing crisis is the result of years of neglect and mismanagement by Enoch Mgijima local municipality, compounded by the misallocation of equitable share grants, which have been primarily used to pay Eskom. Since 2020, the municipality's Eskom debt has skyrocketed from R350 million to an eye-watering R1.4 billion. As a result, a large portion of the municipality's funds is now consumed by debt repayment and staff salaries, leaving little for critical service delivery.
2. The heart of the problem lies in the failure of three key electrical cables that supply power to Top Town, where the Water Works are located. Without power, the pumps cannot deliver water to the town, exacerbating the crisis. One of these cables also supplies power to Frontier Hospital, which has been without electricity and is now relying on backup generators to stay operational. The nearby Madeira Old Age Home is also struggling without power. Just a few days ago, there was a dramatic explosion, and we have footage of this incident, which has been shared with Chwayitisa.
3. The situation has worsened over the last 3.5 weeks, with a series of electrical explosions caused by overloaded cables. In an attempt to address the issue, the municipality has been adding new sections of cable to the existing infrastructure. However, this patchwork approach has only led to more frequent failures. A key issue is the lack of protection systems in the substations—when a fault occurs, it doesn’t just affect one area; it trips the entire town's power grid. This not only disrupts daily life but also inflicts serious and lasting damage to an already fragile infrastructure, further jeopardizing the town's ability to function.
4. What is the current plan? The municipality's current plan involves bringing in new cable sections to extend the old infrastructure, but this is essentially just delaying inevitable failures further down the line.

Lucy Lyons, chairperson of the Madeira Old Age Home Board. It’s located Top Town
1. Located next to the hospital, they are having the issues – they’ve had no electricity for 30 days now. They can only afford to run the generator because of high diesel costs (6-8 AM, 6-8:30 PM). It costs around 16,000 rands for two weeks. Generator can't power washing machines, causing hygiene issues for elderly residents.
2. There’s been cold weather and lack of reheating facilities for the 65 residents who are between 65-95 years old; spoiled food adds to costs, and some residents have gotten sick because they can’t afford to go buy new food. Power outages jeopardize refrigerated medications like insulin and other health-related equipment. There are also hygiene challenges – soiled linen can’t be washed and it's taking a big strain on the staff.
3. The Mayor has been away in China during the crisis, avoiding questions and created confusion. The municipality has had a slow response to power outages in general, unresolved infrastructure problems for over 5 years. Local business owners - Cooks, bakers, and laundromat owners affected by outages.
4. Komani is in a state of decay, and is “literally collapsing”, with Potholes, burnt-down public buildings from protests, and then there’s no power or water- this has created an "apocalyptic" atmosphere.


Further information:
What’s been going on in?
Ken Clark, Owner of Twizza he will talk as one of the biggest business owners of Komani and how devastating it’s been for business owners and for the workers. He took the municipality to court because it needs to be dissolved – they are already under administration but that has failed, so the next step is for it to be dissolved, but province has been trying to prevent that. The court case ended Thursday last week, so now they are waiting for judgement. He’ll talk about the Municipal Manager, Ayakha Mtengenyani, and Executive Mayor, Cllr. Madoda Papiyana, who were in China during the ongoing crisis, attending a solar power conference—an initiative the municipality simply cannot afford. The focus on projects like this, instead of addressing immediate needs, highlights the disconnect between local leadership and the realities on the ground. Under their leadership, there have been several questionable projects, such as the refurbishment of a 6.7 km road, which cost R150 million. The road, primarily used for light vehicle traffic, was over-budgeted by R100 million, with a cost of R16 million per kilometre when it should have cost no more than R50 million in total. He can also talk about the fact that the biggest cost on the municipality’s roll is salaries.
The situation in Komani has become increasingly dire, with a long history of mismanagement and failed interventions. Since the municipality was placed under administration in 2019. Eskom threatened to cut off power to the town but business owners and residents in Komani stepped in to help, making payments on behalf of the municipality, and an agreement was made with Eskom. For a brief period, the municipality honoured this payment plan, but once the COVID-19 pandemic hit, payments stopped altogether. In just 18 months, the municipality’s debt to Eskom skyrocketed from R300 million to R700 million during lockdown – Now its at 1.4billion.
A report at the end of 2022 painted a grim picture of the municipality’s financial health. It revealed that 80% of staff were being overpaid, and there were "ghost workers" on the payroll. The municipality’s revenue collection rate was a mere 55%, meaning that almost half of the funds owed were either being stolen or lost due to damaged infrastructure. Meanwhile, money that should have gone to service delivery was being diverted to salaries.





Extra Budget Items:
Ruan, Sasha and Claire to fly into Queenstown together Sunday and stay until Tuesday (leave that evening).
There will be no electricity - so we need to be prepared for that.

Script:


Visuals start 3-5 seconds before
VO1: Municipal failures in South Africa are nothing new—we’ve seen plenty over the years. But one we keep revisiting is Komani, formerly Queenstown. Just two hours from East London, it feels like a world apart when it comes to functioning properly.
Our first visit in 2018, saw us confront its Municipal Manager about spending R90,000 on fried chicken. It begged the question: better to spend 90k on fried chicken or service delivery?"
upsound: Derek: On your list of priorities is it more important to spend R90,000 on fried chicken or money on cleaning up the townships.
MM: If you compare to what we spend to cleaning up the towns and township each month, that R90,000 is far less.
VO2: It’s that wasteful attitude that saw the Enoch Mgijima Municipality auctioning off assets like garbage trucks and ambulances to cover debt.
Auctioneer and truck nats sound
VO3: In 2019, as the municipality neared collapse, it was placed under administration, meaning the province stepped in to get it back on track.
When we returned ahead of the 2021 local elections, we saw citizens battling waste and corruption…
Claire’s link: The municipality faced social media outrage after announcing the opening of this sports facility - really no more than a fenced field - at a hefty R15 million price tag.
VO4: Three years later we're back to check if the province has made any real progress. The early signs aren’t good as parts of Komani have had no power for over a month, and the treasury looks set to throw another billion at the troubled municipality.
FADE TO BLACK
explosions…
VO5: This isn’t footage from a war zone—it’s a substation exploding, caused by damaged cables and an overloaded electrical grid.
Another explosion (from new facebook - a few)
VO6: Fires at substations (pause) and smouldering power boxes (pause) are an almost daily event, resulting in widespread outages in Komani. In an upscale suburb called Top Town, residents recently lost power for a staggering 35 days.
Alasdair in his kitchen
VO: Alasdair McDonald, a community leader whose lived here for 30 years has found himself at the heart of the blasts. [upsound]
Alasdair and Masa meet at his house, walk outside[

Alasdair: This is a bit of a war zone where a lot of the explosions have been taking place, here, this tree is half dead from an explosion that took place a few nights ago.
Alasdair: There should be four lines feeding up into Top Town here, and they've been relying for many years on only one, that failed spectacularly and we repaired it. We put in joint after joint, and they just continued blowing.
VO: When the power goes down, so do many water pumps - leaving residents high and dry.
Alasdair: So outside of no power, we've had probably 15 days of no water either. (Clipped)
VO: The community wants Komani's entire electricity grid replaced, but the municipality only replaces the burnt cables, leaving a trail of trenches.
Pause
Generators sounds [black screen, fade up]
MASA LINK: If that isn’t the sweet sound of a generator. This has become the soundtrack of Komani.

VO: At Frontier Hospital also in Top Town, it’s the sound of life support. During outages, the hospital relies on five generators. When one failed last month, the consequences were reportedly deadly.
Insider: There were no x-rays, theatre wasn't able to run, and apparently two children passed away.
VO: This hospital insider, whose actual answers are being spoken to us by an actor, says the children's deaths were apparently caused by a lack of power to ventilators.
Insider: The story in the corridors are ventilators stopped, oxygen supply was halted.
Masa: What response are you getting?
Insider: Nothing
Masa: What do you mean?
Insider: It's as if it didn't happen.

VO: Frontier Hospital is meant to provide specialist services to nearly a million people from Komani and beyond. But several sources told us it’s failing at the most basic level.

Insider: I think the biggest issue in the hospital currently is not having linen for theatre. You can go into casualty right now and you'll see people lying on the floor they've been there for weeks
Masa: You can't operate because there's no linen?
Insider: Yes.
Masa: And because you can't operate, there's more people who are now stuck on the floor.
Insider: Yes, on the floor. (SEE PATIENTS ON THE FLOOR IN UNDERCOVER FOOTAGE)
VO: We went undercover in the casualty ward, where toilets are out of order, there are no privacy curtains, and piles of unwashed linen are lying around. It’s hard to see how patients’ dignity can survive here.
VO: A lack of clean linen, compounded by a shortage of qualified staff, means the operating theatre closes at 4pm for all surgeries, except emergency childbirth procedures.
Insider: If a provincial hospital doesn't work at the theatre after hours, they are just as good as a clinic.
Masa: Wait, the theatre doesn't operate after hours?
Insider: Yup, only for obstetrics, cause those patients will sue you if you lose their child.
VO: We called the hospital’s clinical manager.

Masa: There’s allegations of two infants dying because the ventilators went off.
Dr: I’m not in a position to talk about that neh?
Masa: So you are aware of that incident that occurred with the two infants?
Dr. Can I give you the number for my CEO?

VO: So we called the CEO who was in a meeting.

CALL: No one told me that anyone died.
Masa: Do you know anything about the issues of not having curtains in the casualty, not having linen, the theatre not operating functionally?
CEO: No, the theatre operates 24 hours. We are doing caesarean sections. I’m just here, recently, from September.
Masa: So you might want to check up on that?
CEO: Ja.

VO: The Eastern Cape Department of Health dismissed the deaths as fake news, but say they will investigate the other claims. Meanwhile, staff wait for the next explosion to plunge them into darkness again.

PAUSE
VO: With Komani in crisis, you’d expect leadership to stand by its residents?
VO: Well… the municipality recently posted these photos of current Mayor, Madoda Papiyana, on a tour of China, allegedly to secure investments. But it’s this one of the mayor celebrating his birthday that really sparked fury. Because nothing says "I’m working hard for the people" like blowing out candles while they’re lighting them! [About Mayor’s photo: 07:26 Can we maybe blur the background pics slightly, or even desaturate... just to make the front one stand out a bit]
Alasdair: During this crisis of 35 days of no power the mayor was missing in action in China. Paid for by the taxpayer.
Masa: We’re looking forward to having an interview with the mayor as well but we also hear that they don’t really like doing interviews.
Alasdair: If I was running a show like this, I'd probably disappear as well!
Unsurprisingly, the Mayor was once again missing in action.
VO: LINK: We requested an interview with the mayor, but they’ve sent us the acting mayor. Not sure why, but we have plenty of questions.
Intv: Unathi: Today he had to attend a meeting in East London.
Masa: It just seems that the mayor is avoiding accountability?
Unathi: I don't think um I'll be able to answer your question because the question is directed to him personally…

Masa: There's this ongoing electricity crisis, what is going on in this municipality?
Unathi: The infrastructure of the municipality is old.
Masa: Why wasn't it maintained all along anyway?
Unathi: I'm saying that that is a challenge.
Masa: But don't you think it's a self imposed challenge? It's you as the municipality that's not maintaining it.
Unathi: Yes, we understand that there are outages sometimes in the CBDs but the crisis is not in the CBD the crisis is in one of our residential areas. (clipped)
VO: So according to the municipality, the situation isn’t desperate. Well, Lucy Lyons Chair of Madeira Old Age home, disagrees.

Masa: You know how a society treats the elderly is always telling.
Lucy: Our mayor stated that you know Top Town is just a residential area but it's not, we house a government hospital, we've got an old age home. We've got people that got small businesses.
VO: The home is also in the suburb of TopTown and cares for 65 elderly residents, some of whom are in their nineties.
VO: The electricity crisis has put elderly residents at risk, as life saving medications can’t be properly refrigerated.

Lucy: We've got a lot of diabetic patients, so insulin and that's gotta be kept obviously at a certain temperature, and four hours a day from the generator it's not enough to bring those fridges up to temperature.
VO: And the decay spreads far beyond Top Town.

Komani’s Town Hall burned down in 2022 and hasn’t been repaired. The streets are riddled with potholes, rubbish, and raw sewage.
At this local picnic spot outside the city center, millions are spent on security each year.
Alasdair: It certainly appears to be gunshots um
Masa: Just from the upkeep that I mean look at those grass all the way up to my knees.
Alasdair: It speaks for itself doesn't it? Human faeces all around.
Masa: It really stinks, shall we continue outside? (Masa’s horror face)
Alasdair: Absolutely.
Masa: I can’t.

Masa walking out as transition

VO: Most of the municipality’s revenue goes toward an Eskom debt, which has soared from R350 million to R1.4 billion since 2020.
National Treasury is about to pour a billion rand into what some might call a lost cause, in the form of debt relief.

VO: In the meantime, the municipality has developed a power plan.

Kalada: Let's remove the whole cable and then put the new one. The areas in Top Town have got electricity.
Masa: So by the end of this month these areas will have the power back?
Unathi: Definitely.
VISUALLY TRANSITION BACK TO TOP TOWN
LINK: So we just got back from our interview with the acting mayor… The electricity switched on for a few hours last night, but then in the early hours of the morning there was another explosion and now we are back to no electricity.
VO: So, what’s next for this struggling municipality, which has shown little improvement under administration? Perhaps the answer lies in a court case, where a prominent local businessman is challenging the government to have Enoch Mgijima’s leadership completely dissolved. In the meantime, residents will have to wait for that ruling, expected in 2025.

As a result, a large portion of the municipality's funds is now consumed by debt repayment and staff salaries, leaving little for critical service delivery. 2. The heart of the problem lies in the failure of three key electrical cables that supply power to Top Town, where the Water Works are located. Without power, the pumps cannot deliver water to the town, exacerbating the crisis. One of these cables also supplies power to Frontier Hospital, which has been without electricity and is now relying on backup generators to stay operational. The nearby Madeira Old Age Home is also struggling without power. Just a few days ago, there was a dramatic explosion, and we have footage of this incident, which has been shared with Chwayitisa. 3. The situation has worsened over the last 3.5 weeks, with a series of electrical explosions caused by overloaded cables. In an attempt to address the issue, the municipality has been adding new sections of cable to the existing infrastructure. However, this patchwork approach has only led to more frequent failures. A key issue is the lack of protection systems in the substations—when a fault occurs, it doesn’t just affect one area; it trips the entire town's power grid. This not only disrupts daily life but also inflicts serious and lasting damage to an already fragile infrastructure, further jeopardizing the town's ability to function. 4. What is the current plan? But one we keep revisiting is Komani, formerly Queenstown. Just two hours from East London, it feels like a world apart when it comes to functioning properly. Our first visit in 2018, saw us confront its Municipal Manager about spending R90,000 on fried chicken. It begged the question: better to spend 90k on fried chicken or service delivery?" upsound: Derek: On your list of priorities is it more important to spend R90,000 on fried chicken or money on cleaning up the townships. MM: If you compare to what we spend to cleaning up the towns and township each month, that R90,000 is far less. VO2: It’s that wasteful attitude that saw the Enoch Mgijima Municipality auctioning off assets like garbage trucks and ambulances to cover debt. Auctioneer and truck nats sound VO3: In 2019, as the municipality neared collapse, it was placed under administration, meaning the province stepped in to get it back on track. When we returned ahead of the 2021 local elections, we saw citizens battling waste and corruption… Claire’s link: The municipality faced social media outrage after announcing the opening of this sports facility - really no more than a fenced field - at a hefty R15 million price tag. VO4: Three years later we're back to check if the province has made any real progress. The early signs aren’t good as parts of Komani have had no power for over a month, and the treasury looks set to throw another billion at the troubled municipality. FADE TO BLACK explosions… VO5: This isn’t footage from a war zone—it’s a substation exploding, caused by damaged cables and an overloaded electrical grid. Another explosion (from new facebook - a few) VO6: Fires at substations (pause) and smouldering power boxes (pause) are an almost daily event, resulting in widespread outages in Komani. In an upscale suburb called Top Town, residents recently lost power for a staggering 35 days. Alasdair in his kitchen VO: Alasdair McDonald, a community leader whose lived here for 30 years has found himself at the heart of the blasts. [upsound] Alasdair and Masa meet at his house, walk outside[ Alasdair: This is a bit of a war zone where a lot of the explosions have been taking place, here, this tree is half dead from an explosion that took place a few nights ago. Alasdair: There should be four lines feeding up into Top Town here, and they've been relying for many years on only one, that failed spectacularly and we repaired it. We put in joint after joint, and they just continued blowing. VO: When the power goes down, so do many water pumps - leaving residents high and dry. Alasdair: So outside of no power, we've had probably 15 days of no water either. (Clipped) VO: The community wants Komani's entire electricity grid replaced, but the municipality only replaces the burnt cables, leaving a trail of trenches. Pause Generators sounds [black screen, fade up] MASA LINK: If that isn’t the sweet sound of a generator. This has become the soundtrack of Komani. VO: At Frontier Hospital also in Top Town, it’s the sound of life support. During outages, the hospital relies on five generators. When one failed last month, the consequences were reportedly deadly. Insider: There were no x-rays, theatre wasn't able to run, and apparently two children passed away. VO: This hospital insider, whose actual answers are being spoken to us by an actor, says the children's deaths were apparently caused by a lack of power to ventilators. Insider: The story in the corridors are ventilators stopped, oxygen supply was halted. Masa: What response are you getting? Insider: Nothing Masa: What do you mean? Insider: It's as if it didn't happen. VO: Frontier Hospital is meant to provide specialist services to nearly a million people from Komani and beyond. But several sources told us it’s failing at the most basic level. Insider: I think the biggest issue in the hospital currently is not having linen for theatre. You can go into casualty right now and you'll see people lying on the floor they've been there for weeks Masa: You can't operate because there's no linen? Insider: Yes. Masa: And because you can't operate, there's more people who are now stuck on the floor. Insider: Yes, on the floor. (SEE PATIENTS ON THE FLOOR IN UNDERCOVER FOOTAGE) VO: We went undercover in the casualty ward, where toilets are out of order, there are no privacy curtains, and piles of unwashed linen are lying around. It’s hard to see how patients’ dignity can survive here. VO: A lack of clean linen, compounded by a shortage of qualified staff, means the operating theatre closes at 4pm for all surgeries, except emergency childbirth procedures. Insider: If a provincial hospital doesn't work at the theatre after hours, they are just as good as a clinic. Masa: Wait, the theatre doesn't operate after hours? Insider: Yup, only for obstetrics, cause those patients will sue you if you lose their child. VO: We called the hospital’s clinical manager. Masa: There’s allegations of two infants dying because the ventilators went off. Dr: I’m not in a position to talk about that neh? Masa: So you are aware of that incident that occurred with the two infants? Dr. Can I give you the number for my CEO? VO: So we called the CEO who was in a meeting. CALL: No one told me that anyone died. Masa: Do you know anything about the issues of not having curtains in the casualty, not having linen, the theatre not operating functionally? CEO: No, the theatre operates 24 hours. We are doing caesarean sections. I’m just here, recently, from September. Masa: So you might want to check up on that? CEO: Ja. VO: The Eastern Cape Department of Health dismissed the deaths as fake news, but say they will investigate the other claims. Meanwhile, staff wait for the next explosion to plunge them into darkness again. PAUSE VO: With Komani in crisis, you’d expect leadership to stand by its residents? VO: Well… the municipality recently posted these photos of current Mayor, Madoda Papiyana, on a tour of China, allegedly to secure investments. But it’s this one of the mayor celebrating his birthday that really sparked fury. Because nothing says "I’m working hard for the people" like blowing out candles while they’re lighting them! [About Mayor’s photo: 07:26 Can we maybe blur the background pics slightly, or even desaturate... just to make the front one stand out a bit] Alasdair: During this crisis of 35 days of no power the mayor was missing in action in China. Paid for by the taxpayer. Masa: We’re looking forward to having an interview with the mayor as well but we also hear that they don’t really like doing interviews. Alasdair: If I was running a show like this, I'd probably disappear as well! Unsurprisingly, the Mayor was once again missing in action. VO: LINK: We requested an interview with the mayor, but they’ve sent us the acting mayor. Not sure why, but we have plenty of questions. Intv: Unathi: Today he had to attend a meeting in East London. Masa: It just seems that the mayor is avoiding accountability? Unathi: I don't think um I'll be able to answer your question because the question is directed to him personally… Masa: There's this ongoing electricity crisis, what is going on in this municipality? Unathi: The infrastructure of the municipality is old. Masa: Why wasn't it maintained all along anyway? Unathi: I'm saying that that is a challenge. Masa: But don't you think it's a self imposed challenge? It's you as the municipality that's not maintaining it. Unathi: Yes, we understand that there are outages sometimes in the CBDs but the crisis is not in the CBD the crisis is in one of our residential areas. (clipped) VO: So according to the municipality, the situation isn’t desperate. Well, Lucy Lyons Chair of Madeira Old Age home, disagrees. Masa: You know how a society treats the elderly is always telling. Lucy: Our mayor stated that you know Top Town is just a residential area but it's not, we house a government hospital, we've got an old age home. We've got people that got small businesses. VO: The home is also in the suburb of TopTown and cares for 65 elderly residents, some of whom are in their nineties. VO: The electricity crisis has put elderly residents at risk, as life saving medications can’t be properly refrigerated. Lucy: We've got a lot of diabetic patients, so insulin and that's gotta be kept obviously at a certain temperature, and four hours a day from the generator it's not enough to bring those fridges up to temperature. VO: And the decay spreads far beyond Top Town. Komani’s Town Hall burned down in 2022 and hasn’t been repaired. The streets are riddled with potholes, rubbish, and raw sewage. At this local picnic spot outside the city center, millions are spent on security each year. Alasdair: It certainly appears to be gunshots um Masa: Just from the upkeep that I mean look at those grass all the way up to my knees. Alasdair: It speaks for itself doesn't it? Human faeces all around. Masa: It really stinks, shall we continue outside? (Masa’s horror face) Alasdair: Absolutely. Masa: I can’t. Masa walking out as transition VO: Most of the municipality’s revenue goes toward an Eskom debt, which has soared from R350 million to R1.4 billion since 2020. National Treasury is about to pour a billion rand into what some might call a lost cause, in the form of debt relief. VO: In the meantime, the municipality has developed a power plan. Kalada: Let's remove the whole cable and then put the new one. The areas in Top Town have got electricity. Masa: So by the end of this month these areas will have the power back? Unathi: Definitely. VISUALLY TRANSITION BACK TO TOP TOWN LINK: So we just got back from our interview with the acting mayor… The electricity switched on for a few hours last night, but then in the early hours of the morning there was another explosion and now we are back to no electricity. VO: So, what’s next for this struggling municipality, which has shown little improvement under administration? Perhaps the answer lies in a court case, where a prominent local businessman is challenging the government to have Enoch Mgijima’s leadership completely dissolved. In the meantime, residents will have to wait for that ruling, expected in 2025.
